faqs.a: Cubic meters, the standard volume unit in freight. Carriers use it to price sea and air shipments, because cargo space is limited by volume as well as weight.
Carriers convert volume to a weight equivalent and charge whichever is greater: actual or volumetric. For air freight the divisor is 6000 cm3/kg, which equals multiplying CBM by 167.
faqs.q: Why do carriers charge by volumetric weight?

faqs.a: Air: volumetric kg = CBM x 167. Sea: volumetric kg = CBM x 1000. Couriers (express) often use CBM x 200. Pick the mode matching your shipment in the tool.
faqs.q: What is the difference between air and sea volumetric factors?

faqs.a: Divide the dimensions in cm by 100 to get meters first: 50 x 40 x 30 cm = 0.5 x 0.4 x 0.3 m = 0.06 CBM per box. Or just use this calculator's cm mode.
faqs.q: How do I calculate CBM from cm?

faqs.a: Charges apply to the greater of actual and volumetric weight. A light but bulky item (pillows, for example) is billed on volume; a dense item (books) on actual weight.
faqs.q: Do I pay on actual or volumetric weight?

cbm-calculator.formula:
CBM per piece = length (m) x width (m) x height (m)
total CBM = CBM per piece x quantity
volumetric weight (air) = total CBM x 167 kg
volumetric weight (sea) = total CBM x 1000 kg
chargeable weight = max(actual weight, volumetric weight)

The calculator returns total cubic meters, volumetric weight using the standard carrier factors, and the chargeable weight — the higher of actual and volumetric — that freight is billed on.

cbm-calculator.workedExample:
Two cartons of 50 x 40 x 30 cm, 10 kg each, air freight:

1. Per piece = 0.50 x 0.40 x 0.30 = 0.060 CBM.
2. Total CBM = 0.060 x 2 = 0.120 CBM.
3. Volumetric weight (air) = 0.120 x 167 = 20.04 kg.
4. Actual weight = 10 x 2 = 20 kg.
5. Chargeable weight = max(20, 20.04) = 20.04 kg.

The forwarder bills about 20 kg even though the boxes weigh 20 kg — volume just edges out.
